subject: chemistry

items.q: A life cycle assessment is carried out on a new electric kettle. Which stages of the kettle's life does the assessment cover?
items.correct: Extracting and processing raw materials, manufacture, use, then disposal
items.misconception: Extraction, manufacture, use and disposal, plus transport as a fifth
items.why: The specification names transport at the end of the fourth bullet, so it looks like another item on the list rather than something counted throughout. The words 'at each stage' mean transport is counted inside every stage: carrying ore to a works, parts to a factory, goods to shops and waste to landfill.
items.random_wrong: Manufacturing and packaging only, as that is where pollution comes from

items.q: Why does a manufacturer carry out a life cycle assessment on a new product?
items.correct: To assess the environmental impact of it across its whole life
items.misconception: To measure the pollution given off by the factory that makes it
items.why: Manufacture is the stage students picture most easily and the one shown in textbook images. In everyday speech 'production' is also used loosely to mean the whole life of a product. Manufacturing and packaging is only one of four stages. A product made in a clean factory can still have a large overall impact from extraction, from its use, or from its disposal.
items.random_wrong: To find the profit the product will make once it goes on sale

items.q: An LCA is carried out on a poly(ethene) shopping bag. Which of these is counted in the 'extracting and processing raw materials' stage?
items.correct: Drilling for crude oil and processing it into poly(ethene)
items.misconception: Only the drilling for crude oil, and not the refining that follows it
items.why: Students read 'raw materials' as the material in its natural state and treat everything done to it afterwards as manufacturing. The stage is 'extracting and processing raw materials'. Refining crude oil, reducing an ore and firing clay all belong to it, and they often use far more energy than the extraction itself.
items.random_wrong: Growing and harvesting the plants that most plastics are made from

items.q: An LCA is carried out on a jar of jam sold in a glass jar. Which of these belongs to the 'manufacturing and packaging' stage?
items.correct: Moulding the hot glass and boxing the jars for delivery
items.misconception: Only the work done inside the factory, as transport is its own stage
items.why: The specification names transport at the end of the fourth bullet, so it looks like another item on the list rather than something counted throughout. The words 'at each stage' mean transport is counted inside every stage: carrying ore to a works, parts to a factory, goods to shops and waste to landfill.
items.random_wrong: The cardboard tray is left out, as it is not part of the product

items.q: Two washing machines have the same impacts at every stage but one: machine A uses less electricity and less water per wash. Which stage of the LCA does this difference belong to?
items.correct: Use and operation during its lifetime, as less energy and water are used
items.misconception: No stage at all, since electricity is used at home and not at a works
items.why: Impacts are pictured as smoke from a chimney. Electricity arrives invisibly at a socket, so the generation behind it is forgotten. For appliances such as washing machines and kettles the use stage often dominates the whole LCA, because the energy is consumed over many years.
items.random_wrong: Manufacturing and packaging, since the factory sets how efficient it is

items.q: In an LCA of tinned food, where is the impact of the lorry journeys that carry the tins to the shops counted?
items.correct: Within each stage, since transport is included at all four stages
items.misconception: In a separate transport stage, added on after the four main stages
items.why: The specification names transport at the end of the fourth bullet, so it looks like another item on the list rather than something counted throughout. The words 'at each stage' mean transport is counted inside every stage: carrying ore to a works, parts to a factory, goods to shops and waste to landfill.
items.random_wrong: In manufacturing and packaging, as the factory arranges delivery

items.q: A plastic garden chair is collected and buried in landfill at the end of its life. Which statement about the disposal stage of its LCA is correct?
items.correct: The transport of the chair and the burying of it are counted
items.misconception: Nothing is counted, because a chair sent to landfill is not processed
items.why: Disposal feels like the end of the story, and landfill is out of sight, so students assume nothing further is used. Disposal has its own impacts: lorry journeys, land taken up, and substances leaching from the waste. Recycling routes also use energy of their own.
items.random_wrong: Only the burying counts, since the lorry journey is a separate stage

items.q: Which of these can be quantified fairly easily in a life cycle assessment?
items.correct: The mass of water used to make the item
items.misconception: The harm a pollutant does to a nearby river
items.why: Students know pollutant concentrations can be measured, and do not distinguish measuring the amount released from valuing the harm it causes. The mass of a pollutant can be measured, but deciding how much damage that mass does, and how it compares with a different pollutant, requires a value judgement.
items.random_wrong: How strongly local people object to the works

items.q: Why is a life cycle assessment not a purely objective process?
items.correct: Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires value judgements
items.misconception: Because different scientists measure the energy used in different units
items.why: Numbers look objective, and students expect a calculation in science to have a single right answer. Some quantities are measured, but the weight given to different pollutant effects is judged, not measured. Two assessors can weigh the same data differently and reach different conclusions.
items.random_wrong: Because the mass of waste made can never be measured accurately

items.q: Two teams carry out a full LCA on the same paint and reach opposite conclusions, although both used the same measured data for water, energy and waste. What is the best explanation?
items.correct: The teams gave the pollutant effects of this paint different weights
items.misconception: One of the two teams must have made an arithmetic error somewhere
items.why: Numbers look objective, and students expect a calculation in science to have a single right answer. Some quantities are measured, but the weight given to different pollutant effects is judged, not measured. Two assessors can weigh the same data differently and reach different conclusions.
items.random_wrong: Pollutant effects cannot go into an LCA at all, so both teams guessed

items.q: What is the main risk of using a selective or abbreviated LCA?
items.correct: It can be used to support a conclusion decided beforehand
items.misconception: It gives less accurate figures, as fewer decimal places are used
items.why: Students treat a shorter study as a rougher version of the same thing, rather than as one whose choice of stages can be biased. The problem is not precision but selection. If the stages where a product performs badly are omitted, the remaining numbers can be accurate and the conclusion still misleading.
items.random_wrong: It removes all of the value judgements from the assessment

items.q: An advert calls a new drinks carton 'the greenest on the market', citing an LCA that assessed only the manufacturing stage. Which criticism of the claim is valid?
items.correct: Stages that favour rival cartons have been left out
items.misconception: Advertising claims can never be based on data from an LCA
items.why: Students know pollutant concentrations can be measured, and do not distinguish measuring the amount released from valuing the harm it causes. The mass of a pollutant can be measured, but deciding how much damage that mass does, and how it compares with a different pollutant, requires a value judgement.
items.random_wrong: Manufacturing impacts cannot be quantified in a reliable way

items.q: A comparative LCA of a plastic bag and a paper bag shows that the paper bag needs more energy and more water to make. A student concludes that paper bags are worse for the environment. Why is that conclusion unsafe?
items.correct: The remaining stages, including reuse and disposal, have not been considered
items.misconception: Paper comes from trees, so a paper bag can have no impact at all
items.why: Biodegradable and renewable are treated as meaning harmless, and the disposal stage is allowed to decide the whole comparison. A comparative LCA covers every stage. Paper bags usually lose at the raw materials and manufacturing stages even though they win at disposal.
items.random_wrong: Energy and water use cannot be quantified, so the figures mean little

items.q: In a comparative LCA of shopping bags, which factor has the greatest effect on the environmental impact per use of a bag?
items.correct: The number of times the bag is reused before it is thrown out
items.misconception: Nothing after manufacture, as the impact is fixed at the factory
items.why: Students compare the bags item for item rather than per use, because the manufacturing figures are the ones given in the data. Compare impact per use. A heavier bag reused fifty times can easily beat a light bag that is used once and thrown away.
items.random_wrong: Whether the material will break down in a landfill site

items.q: In a simple comparative LCA, why can a paper shopping bag have a greater impact than a plastic one at the raw materials and manufacturing stages?
items.correct: More energy and water are needed to turn the wood into paper
items.misconception: Paper rots away, and biodegradable materials cost more to manufacture
items.why: Biodegradable and renewable are treated as meaning harmless, and the disposal stage is allowed to decide the whole comparison. A comparative LCA covers every stage. Paper bags usually lose at the raw materials and manufacturing stages even though they win at disposal.
items.random_wrong: Plastic bags come from a renewable source, but paper bags do not

items.q: Which action by an end user reduces the use of limited resources by the greatest amount?
items.correct: Buying fewer new products in the first place
items.misconception: Recycling each product carefully after using it once
items.why: Recycling is the most visible action, with bins and collections, while using less is invisible and is not organised for you. Recycling still needs collection, transport and reprocessing, all of which use energy. Reduction avoids the impacts altogether, and reuse avoids the reprocessing.
items.random_wrong: Choosing products whose packaging can be recycled

items.q: Aluminium drinks cans are collected and recycled instead of being replaced by new aluminium extracted from its ore. Which statement about this is correct?
items.correct: Less ore has to be mined and far less energy is needed overall
items.misconception: Recycling the cans needs no energy at all, unlike extraction
items.why: Recycling is presented as the green option, so students treat its impact as zero rather than as reduced. Recycling reduces impact; it does not remove it. Melting scrap metal or glass still needs a large amount of energy, much of which comes from limited resources.
items.random_wrong: Aluminium ore becomes renewable once the cans are recycled

items.q: Which statement about the raw materials used to make metals, glass, clay ceramics and most plastics is correct?
items.correct: They all come from limited raw materials found in the Earth
items.misconception: Most plastics are made from plants, so they are a renewable source
items.why: Plant-based and compostable plastics are advertised heavily, and students generalise from those examples. A few plastics are made from plant material, but the specification treats most plastics as produced from limited raw materials, which is why plastic use is a resource issue.
items.random_wrong: They are unlimited, because these products can be recycled

items.q: A company quarries limestone to make cement. Which of these is the best description of the environmental impact of the quarrying?
items.correct: Dust, noise and the loss of habitat around the quarry site
items.misconception: There is no lasting impact, as the site will be landscaped later
items.why: Company photographs of restored sites suggest that the damage has been undone. Restoration reduces the lasting damage to the landscape, but the impacts during the working life of the quarry, and the loss of the material removed, cannot be undone.
items.random_wrong: The only impact is the fuel burned by the machines there

items.q: A glass bottle is returned to the dairy, washed and then filled with milk again. Which term describes what has happened to the bottle, and why?
items.correct: Reuse, because the bottle is used again as it is
items.misconception: Recycling, because the glass has been used for a second time
items.why: In everyday speech 'reuse' covers anything that is not thrown away, and both routes start at the same bottle bank. Reuse means the object itself is used again, like a bottle washed and refilled. If the material is melted and reshaped, that is recycling.
items.random_wrong: Reduction, because fewer new bottles now need making

items.q: Waste glass bottles are crushed and melted, and the glass is then made into new glass jars. Why is this recycling rather than reuse?
items.correct: The glass has been reprocessed and made into a different product
items.misconception: It is reuse, because the same glass is being used once more
items.why: In everyday speech 'reuse' covers anything that is not thrown away, and both routes start at the same bottle bank. Reuse means the object itself is used again, like a bottle washed and refilled. If the material is melted and reshaped, that is recycling.
items.random_wrong: Recycled glass must always be turned back into bottles

items.q: How are metals recycled?
items.correct: They are melted and then recast or reformed into products
items.misconception: They are reused directly without any melting or processing
items.why: Recycling is presented as the green option, so students treat its impact as zero rather than as reduced. Recycling reduces impact; it does not remove it. Melting scrap metal or glass still needs a large amount of energy, much of which comes from limited resources.
items.random_wrong: They are melted only when every metal has been separated

items.q: At a steelworks, some scrap steel is added to the molten iron that comes from a blast furnace. Why is this done?
items.correct: It cuts the amount of iron that must be extracted from ore
items.misconception: It acts as a fuel in the furnace, so less coke has to be burned
items.why: Everything else added to a blast furnace, such as coke, is there to react, so students assume the scrap reacts too; and 'reduce the amount' is read as 'remove the need'. The scrap is melted by the heat of the hot iron and adds to the mass of metal produced. Ore is still used, but less of it for each tonne of steel made.
items.random_wrong: It removes the need to use any iron ore at the works at all

items.q: A council has data on four schemes. New raw material avoided each year: repair scheme 900 t, kerbside recycling 400 t, recycled bin bags 120 t, burning waste 0 t. Which scheme cuts the use of limited resources the most?
items.correct: A repair scheme for household goods
items.misconception: Kerbside recycling of bottles and cans
items.why: Recycling is the most visible action, with bins and collections, while using less is invisible and is not organised for you. Recycling still needs collection, transport and reprocessing, all of which use energy. Reduction avoids the impacts altogether, and reuse avoids the reprocessing.
items.random_wrong: Bin bags made from recycled waste

items.q: A plastic bag needs 0.6 MJ to make and is used once. A paper bag needs 2.0 MJ to make and is reused 4 times. What is the energy used per use of the paper bag?
items.correct: 0.5 MJ
items.misconception: 2.0 MJ
items.why: Students compare the bags item for item rather than per use, because the manufacturing figures are the ones given in the data. Compare impact per use. A heavier bag reused fifty times can easily beat a light bag that is used once and thrown away.
items.random_wrong: 8.0 MJ

items.q: A comparative LCA gives the energy to make each bag: paper 2.0 MJ, plastic 0.6 MJ. A shopper reuses a paper bag 10 times and uses a plastic bag once. Which conclusion do these figures support?
items.correct: Per use the paper bag uses less energy than the plastic bag
items.misconception: The plastic bag uses less energy per use than the paper
items.why: Students compare the bags item for item rather than per use, because the manufacturing figures are the ones given in the data. Compare impact per use. A heavier bag reused fifty times can easily beat a light bag that is used once and thrown away.
items.random_wrong: Energy use cannot be quantified, so the figures prove nothing

items.q: Is packaging assessed in an LCA?
items.correct: Yes. The second stage is manufacturing and packaging, so the resources and energy used to make the packaging are counted.
items.misconception: Packaging is thrown away straight away, so it is only counted at the disposal stage, or not at all.
items.why: Packaging is not the thing the customer wants, so students do not think of it as part of the product being assessed. Packaging is named in the second stage. Its raw materials, manufacture, transport and disposal all add to the total impact.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the material for a plastic bag come from?
items.correct: Most plastics are polymers made from crude oil, which is a limited raw material.
items.misconception: Plastic bags are made from a renewable source, or plastic must lose to paper at every single stage.
items.why: 'Plastic is bad' is a strong everyday message, so students assume it loses every comparison, and the small mass of a plastic bag is overlooked. Plastics come from crude oil, but a plastic bag is light and quick to make, so it can use less energy and water at the manufacturing stage than a paper one.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are metal ores a limited resource?
items.correct: Yes. Ores are limited raw materials obtained from the Earth, which is one reason why recycling metals matters.
items.misconception: Metals can be recycled over and over, so the supply of metal is unlimited and ores will not run out.
items.why: Recycling is described as endless, and students transfer that idea to the raw material itself. Recycling slows the rate at which ore is used, but metal is still lost in use and in waste, and any new metal must come from a limited supply of ore.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must a recycled material be made into the same product again?
items.correct: No. Products that cannot be reused are recycled for a different use, for example glass bottles crushed and melted to make different glass products.
items.misconception: Recycled glass has to be made into new bottles, and recycled metal into the same object it came from.
items.why: Recycling logos and adverts show a closed loop leading back to the identical product. The recycled material is often used for something else, because a different product may need less separation, or less purity, than the original one did.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How much separation is needed before scrap is recycled?
items.correct: It depends on the material and on the properties required of the final product; some uses need carefully sorted scrap and others do not.
items.misconception: All scrap must be sorted into completely pure separate metals before any of it can be recycled.
items.why: Students know mixtures are impure and assume purity is always required, and school recycling stresses careful sorting. The purity needed is set by the job the metal must do. Scrap steel added to iron from a blast furnace needs little separation; metal for an alloy of fixed composition needs much more.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the rocks and ores taken by quarrying replace themselves?
items.correct: No. They form far too slowly to be replaced on any human timescale, so they are limited raw materials.
items.misconception: Rock and sand are everywhere and keep forming, so quarrying limestone or clay is sustainable.
items.why: The rock cycle is taught as a continuous process, and students do not appreciate the timescale involved. Rock formation takes millions of years. Limestone, ores and clay are all limited raw materials, and they are being removed far faster than they form.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the environmental impacts of mining and quarrying?
items.correct: They include loss of habitat, dust, noise, spoil heaps and polluted water, as well as the energy used and the transport involved.
items.misconception: The only impact of quarrying is the fuel burned by the machinery.
items.why: Environmental impact is often equated with carbon dioxide alone, so effects on land, water and wildlife are overlooked. Extraction damages the local environment directly. The land is dug away, habitats are destroyed, and dust and noise affect the surrounding area as well.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.10.2 Life cycle assessment and recycling
